headline: Every big AI report last night beat and every one is being sold this morning: Meta lifted its capex floor, Tesla cut its spending and Lam guided flat, while a deadly drone strike in Saudi Arabia pushed Brent back above $111 and China's main index fell into a bear market.
summary: The dashboard now has Wednesday Oct 21 closes, so verdicts, zones and setups below are current to that close. Wednesday was a good day: the S&P 500 rose 0.58% to 7,757.17 and the Nasdaq about 1%, helped by SpaceX and Capital One. Then the night turned it around. Meta beat on sales and raised its 2026 capex floor to $135 billion but gave no 2027 number and had negative free cash flow; Tesla beat but cut 2026 capex to about $20 billion; Lam guided in line and fell about 7% to 8%. A Houthi drone strike on Saudi Aramco's Shaybah field killed two people, Brent rose as much as 3.3% to $112.43, and S&P 500 futures were down 1.1% at 7:16am ET. The Bank of Korea held at 3.00% and the KOSPI fell 3.52%. The dashboard still has no swing or put setups, and no put idea passes.

regime.why: Four AI reports beat and all four stocks fell before the open, which says buyers are tired of paying for AI spending they cannot yet see a return on. Oil is back above $110 on a deadly attack inside Saudi Arabia, and China's CSI 300 is in a bear market. Breadth was fine on Wednesday, so this is a day to sit on your hands, not to panic: no new buys into a gap down.

signals.title: Meta, Tesla, Lam and IBM all beat and all fell: Meta raised its 2026 capex floor to $135 billion but gave no 2027 number, Tesla cut its spending, and Lam guided flat
signals.since_yesterday: Meta's number is in: 2026 capex of $135 to $145 billion (up from $130 to $145 billion), no 2027 outlook, and negative free cash flow in Q3. Every AI report last night was sold.
signals.what_happened: Meta (META) after Wednesday's close: revenue $64.6 billion, up 26%, against about $63.3 billion expected; Q4 revenue guide $73 to $76 billion. It narrowed 2026 capex to $135 to $145 billion from $130 to $145 billion and said it is not giving a 2027 capex outlook yet; FactSet analysts had about $196 billion for 2027. Q3 capex was $34.9 billion and free cash flow was about negative $2.1 billion. A $9.9 billion legal charge from the teen safety settlement cut reported profit, and 2026 total expenses are now $175 to $179 billion. Meta will also issue non voting Class C shares, one for each Class A and B share, effective Jan 19, 2027: in effect a 2 for 1 split that lets it raise money for AI without diluting Zuckerberg's vote. META closed at 697.52 on Oct 21, rose about 2.5% after hours, and was about 1% lower premarket. Tesla (TSLA): adjusted EPS $0.48 against about $0.43, revenue about $28.05 billion, gross margin 19.6%, free cash flow $1.53 billion, down 62%. On the call it cut 2026 capex to about $20 billion from more than $25 billion, said Optimus production has started on high volume lines in Fremont with a slow, bumpy ramp, and targets first Cybercab customer deliveries by Dec 31. TSLA closed at 386.47 and was down about 3% to 5% premarket. Lam Research (LRCX): record September quarter revenue of $8.22 billion and a record 40.0% operating margin, but the December guide of $8.60 billion, plus or minus $400 million, sits only $30 million above consensus; the CFO blamed supply chain limits, and China falls from 35% of sales. LRCX closed at 260.81 and fell about 7% to 8% overnight. IBM fell 5.7% premarket after a beat and a raised cash flow outlook. Nokia this morning: AI and cloud customer sales up 123%, optical networks up 18%. At 7:16am ET, S&P 500 futures were down 1.1% and Nasdaq 100 futures 1.7%.
signals.so_what: Follow the money. The spenders are still spending: Meta's floor went up and TSMC, Nokia and Lam all report rising AI orders. What changed is who is willing to fund it. Meta now burns cash on its build and is creating a new share class to raise money; Tesla is spending less on factories and more on robots. When the biggest buyers turn cash negative, investors start pricing the risk that 2027 budgets flatten, and the suppliers with the most China exposure and the least pricing power (equipment makers like Lam) get hit first. Chokepoint owners with sold out capacity (TSMC, memory, Nvidia) are better placed than tool makers. What would make this wrong: a clear 2027 capex number from Microsoft, Alphabet or Amazon next week that rises again.
signals.for_you: Swing: none. The dashboard has no swing setups on Oct 21 closes, and you do not buy into a gap down. Long term: NVDA moved up to 'Buy zone now' at 221.97 (zone 197.03 to 229.60, buyers lead at 1.06) and MRVL stays 'Buy zone now' at 244.76, but wait for a close after today's selling before adding; a small first tranche only. LRCX stays Wait at 260.81, below its 274.28 zone bottom and close to the 254.48 thesis line: no buys. TSLA is Avoid at 386.47. META is Wait at 697.52 (46% above fair value). Puts: none on any of these into this gap.

signals.title: A Houthi drone strike on Saudi Arabia's Shaybah field killed two people and the US ordered some embassy staff out; Brent jumped as high as $112.43 and American Airlines shows the fuel bill
signals.since_yesterday: The attacks moved inside Saudi Arabia with deaths at Shaybah and Dammam airport, and the US ordered some embassy staff to leave. Iran's mine claims are no longer the main driver.
signals.what_happened: Brent added 3 cents to settle at $108.82 on Oct 21 and WTI fell 67 cents to $97.15 (CNBC). Overnight, a drone strike on Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field killed two people but did not affect operations, a separate attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed one, and the US ordered some embassy staff and family members to leave the kingdom (Bloomberg). Brent rose as much as 3.3% to $112.43 early Thursday (CNBC) and traded near $111 to $112 (OilPrice.com). President Trump denied the US is negotiating with Iran but said the war could end soon; Iran says indirect talks continue through Pakistan and Qatar. CENTCOM says its escorted corridor has restored about 80% of prewar Hormuz traffic. American Airlines this morning: record Q3 revenue of $16.3 billion, up 19.3%, but fuel expense up $1.9 billion, or 67.5%, and an adjusted loss of $0.28 a share, inside its guided range.
signals.so_what: Shaybah is deep in the Saudi desert, far from Hormuz. A strike there says the Houthis can reach Saudi oil fields, which means the Saudi bypass routes are not a safe backup. That is why the premium came back even though no barrels were lost. Who pays: airlines and anyone who buys fuel. American's revenue grew almost 20% and it still lost money. Who gets paid: US producers with no Gulf exposure. The 2019 Abqaiq attack is the guide: the spike faded once output came back. Here output was not hit, so the risk is the next strike, not this one.
signals.for_you: Swing: if you hold energy swings, keep the dashboard stops and do not add on a headline gap. Oct 21 closes: XOM 178.09, CVX 226.78, COP 145.67, EOG 157.88; buyers still lead (up/down 1.11 to 1.34), and all four beat SPY over 3 months. Airlines: UAL stays Avoid at 101.67; DAL is 'Buy zone, wait for the chart' at 77.67 with sellers leading (0.92). AAL has no dashboard verdict. No airline puts while oil swings $3 a day.

signals.title: Lockheed beat and raised on a record $292 billion backlog, $52.5 billion of it Patriot interceptors; Hexcel's airplane sales rose 21%
signals.what_happened: Lockheed Martin (LMT) this morning: Q3 sales $20.7 billion, up from $18.6 billion, with growth in all four segments; EPS $7.97 against about $7.50 expected; free cash flow $3.0 billion. Backlog hit a record $292.0 billion, including $52.5 billion from the multiyear PAC-3 MSE interceptor award. It raised 2026 guidance to sales of about $80 to $82 billion, EPS of $30.35 to $30.75 and free cash flow of $7.8 to $8.0 billion, and raised its dividend for the 24th straight year. LMT closed at 551.51 on Oct 21. Hexcel (HXL) after Wednesday's close: sales $496 million, up 8.8%; adjusted EPS $0.50 against $0.37 a year ago; commercial aerospace sales up 20.5% to $330.3 million, while defense, space and other fell 8.7% to $166.1 million. It kept its 2026 guidance and raised its buyback authorization to $750 million. The call is at 9:30am ET today.
signals.so_what: Follow the interceptor money. Every missile fired in the Gulf has to be replaced, and the Pentagon is now signing multiyear deals to do it: RTX ($340 billion), Northrop (a record $109.6 billion) and now Lockheed (a record $292 billion) all reported big backlogs this week. That is cash locked in for years, which is why defense held up on bad days. For Hexcel, the carbon fiber in every new jet, the signal is Boeing and Airbus rate increases showing up as orders; the soft spot is fighter and space programs. What would make this wrong: a ceasefire that slows replenishment, or a budget fight after the Nov 3 election.
signals.for_you: Long term: LMT sits inside its buy zone (543.22 to 555.53) at 551.51 on Oct 21 but is 'Buy zone, wait for the chart' because sellers led (up/down 0.95). A strong close today on heavy volume could flip that; do not buy before the close confirms. NOC is 'Accumulate on pullback' at 539.31. HXL is Wait at 89.84 (72% above fair value). Swing: none. Puts: no LMT put while the verdict is not 'Buy zone now'.

signals.title: World check: the Bank of Korea held and hinted at more hikes, the KOSPI fell 3.52%, China's CSI 300 entered a bear market, and France's 10 year yield crossed 5% the day before Moody's
signals.since_yesterday: The Bank of Korea held at 3.00% as expected but signaled more tightening, and Seoul gave back Wednesday's rebound. French yields hit a 24 year high.
signals.what_happened: Korea: all seven Bank of Korea board members voted to hold at 3.00% after hikes in July and August; Governor Shin said further hikes depend on Q3 GDP and inflation, and most watchers expect two more through next year (JoongAng Daily, CNBC). The KOSPI fell 3.52% to 5,533.77, its lowest close since April, as chip stocks were sold (Seoul Economic Daily). China: the CSI 300 closed 20.2% below its June 22 peak, its first bear market since 2020, after 10 straight weekly losses (Bloomberg via Yahoo). Japan, Taiwan and Hong Kong fell about 2% to 3% in reports during the session; closing levels were not confirmed. France: the 10 year yield touched 5% on Oct 21, up 8 basis points, its highest since 2002 (Reuters), and reached about 5.10% on Oct 22 (FXStreet); the gap over German bonds is near its widest since 2011. Moody's rates France Aa3 with a negative outlook and reviews it on Friday Oct 23. Brazil: Quaest (released Oct 21) has Flavio Bolsonaro at 45% and Lula at 44%, narrower than its 46% to 44% a week earlier (Reuters); the runoff is Sunday.
signals.so_what: Asia is where the AI doubt shows first, because its markets are full of chip and server makers. A central bank that holds but says it may hike again, plus a stronger won, is a double hit to Korean exporters. A bear market in China's top 300 stocks adds pressure on anyone selling into China. In France, bond buyers are already pricing a downgrade, so a Moody's cut on Friday would confirm, not shock; no cut would be a relief. Brazil is now within one point, so the market's pricing of a Bolsonaro win is riskier than it was.
signals.for_you: No action. KB and SHG are left out of both lists: a hawkish hold helps bank margins but the stock market sell off hurts. NU is 'Buy zone now' at 15.05, exactly at its zone top: no buys or puts until after Sunday's vote. No dashboard name is French.

history.when: 2000 to 2002, the dot com and telecom build out
history.what: The Nasdaq fell from 5,048.62 on March 10, 2000 to 1,114.11 on Oct 9, 2002, about 78%. Internet use kept growing, but builders had funded capacity with debt and new stock, and the money stopped.
history.lesson: When buyers start paying for capacity with new shares instead of cash flow, suppliers get repriced first. Meta's new share class is a step in that direction, not proof of a top.

history.when: September 14 to 16, 2019, the Abqaiq and Khurais attack
history.what: Drones hit Saudi Arabia's Abqaiq processing plant and Khurais field, and Brent jumped about 15% on the first trading day. Most of the gain faded within weeks as Aramco restored output.
history.lesson: Oil spikes on Saudi attacks fade when barrels return. This time no output was lost at Shaybah, so the premium is about the next strike, not this one.

source.title: Saudi attack hits global oil supply, prices surge 15% (Deccan Herald, Sep 2019)

cycle.differences: The 1991 Desert Storm comparison is swapped for 2019 Abqaiq because the attacks are now on Saudi soil, not Hormuz. What is different from 2000: the AI buyers still have real revenue (Meta $64.6 billion a quarter) and the spending floor went up, not down. What is different from 2019: then the attack was a one off; now strikes have hit Saudi targets several times in a week and the US is moving staff out.
